newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU sees low grain export subsidy after farm reform.
newsitem.headline: EU sees low grain export subsidy after farm reform.

text.p: Farmers who rely on European Union subsidies to export their grain must live without them as a rule once new reforms come in, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said in an interview due to be published on Wednesday.

In an advance copy of the interview with Le Figaro supplied to Reuters, Fischler defended proposals to cut EU support prices at the turn of the century without giving full compensation to cereal farmers.
"The current situation is not tenable," Fischler was quoted as saying. "For cereals ... the European Union must without doubt be able, in a normal year, to export without subsidy," he said.
"Do not forget that we are proposing to abolish set-aside," Fischler he said, referrring to a controversial scheme in which farmers are paid not to produce from part of their land.
French farmers have fought for years for the abolition of set-aside but vow to resist cuts in the "intervention" prices used to prop up the domestic market for grain and other goods.
The Commission's latest "Agenda 2000" farm reform, unveiled in Strasbourg last month, would cut these prices for cereals by 20 percent to 95.35 Ecus per tonne from 2000.
Only part of the cut would be offered back to grain farmers in the form of increased payments for each hectare sown.

Lowering domestic prices would tend to make farmers less dependent on export subsidies. They have traditionally depended heavily on such aid since prices on the world market are generally lower than the protected European levels.
However, Fischler's remarks were released on a day when the EU was unusually having to turn the subsidies into taxes on wheat exports to prevent a flood of unwanted foreign sales.
The Commisison earlier on Tuesday raised this tax on wheat exports to three Ecus per tonne from 0.5 Ecus per tonne and doubled a tax on pasta-making durum wheat to 10 Ecus.
Grain export subsidies have been relatively scarce since a global supply scare in 1995 and early 1996 forced European and other world prices to converge for the first time in 20 years.
Though there has been some recovery in grain reserves from 20-year lows, European and world prices remain closely in line.
EU officials fear however that the 15-nation bloc will soon be saddled with large new grain mountains that need subsidies to export unless internal prices come down.
Austrian-born Fischler faces tough negotiations of at least 18 months with EU members before the reforms are accepted.

Complicating his task are plans for new global trade negotiations from 1999. These are seen likely to tighten previous international limits on the use of grain export subsidies or push for them to be phased out altogether.
